html:
A librarian who finds one book among thousands in seconds, a school office that prints every student's marksheet in an afternoon, and a bank that knows your balance the moment you pay with Fonepay all rely on the same idea: data kept in an organised, searchable form.

This unit explains what a database is, how a Database Management System (DBMS) looks after it, and how to build and use one in MySQL with SQL commands.

What the SEE asks from this unit (8 marks)

The SEE specification grid gives this unit 8 marks: two MCQs (2 marks), one short question (2 marks) and one long question (4 marks). MCQs test a key, a data type or which SQL command does what.

The short question is usually a definition with an advantage (DBMS, primary key) or two differences (data and information, DDL and DML).

The long question asks you to define and explain with examples (database, DBMS, fields and records) or to write SQL for a given table — CREATE, INSERT, SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY or LIKE, UPDATE and DELETE.

In SQL answers every keyword, comma, quote and semicolon is a key element, so write each query in full.

2.1 Introduction to database: data, information, database and DBMS

Databases work quietly behind almost everything you do online.

Area What the database stores
Social media user profiles, posts, comments, likes
Online shopping (Daraz, SastoDeal) products, prices, orders, reviews
Banking and wallets (eSewa, Khalti) accounts, transactions, balances
Hospitals patient records, test reports, appointments
Schools students, attendance, marks, fees

Data and information

Data and information

Data are raw facts and figures — numbers, words, dates, images — that have no clear meaning on their own. Information is data that has been organised or processed so that it is meaningful and useful for understanding something or making a decision.

The marks 80, 85 and 90 are data. "Binay's average in the three terminal exams is 85, so he improved by 10 marks" is information: the data has been processed (averaged and compared) and now means something.

Aspect Data Information
Definition raw, unprocessed facts and figures processed, organised data with meaning
Form numbers, text, symbols, images tables, reports, summaries, charts
Meaning no clear meaning on its own meaningful and useful for decisions
Stage input to processing output of processing
Example 2082, 95, Binay "Binay scored 95 in 2082 BS and was among the toppers."

Database

Database

A database is an organised collection of related data stored so that it can be easily accessed, managed and updated. In a relational database the data is kept in tables of rows and columns.

Before computers, records were kept on paper: registers, files in cabinets and card catalogues. This traditional file system works for a few hundred records, but searching, sorting, copying and keeping it correct all depend on human effort.

Traditional (manual) file system Computerised database
records on paper in registers and cabinets records stored digitally in tables
slow to search, sort and update searching and sorting take seconds
the same data copied in many files (redundancy) data stored once and shared
copies easily disagree (inconsistency) rules keep the data consistent
hard to protect; one fire destroys it passwords, permissions and backups
one person can use a file at a time many users at the same time
Group activity

In groups, collect the name, age and favourite subject of five classmates and arrange the data as a small table.

Then discuss: if the school had 1,000 students, what would be hard about the paper version, and how would a DBMS make searching ("all students who like Computer"), sorting and updating easier?

Database Management System (DBMS)

DBMS

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software used to create, store, retrieve, update and delete data in a database in an organised way, while keeping the data correct (integrity), safe (security) and available to many users.

It works as the intermediary between the users and the database.

Examples of DBMS software: MySQL (open source, used by most websites), Oracle Database (commercial, large enterprises), Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL (open source, advanced features), SQLite (tiny, built into phones and apps) and MongoDB (a NoSQL system for unstructured data).

Recent trends. Cloud databases run on the Internet and grow with your needs (Google Cloud SQL, Amazon RDS). NoSQL databases such as MongoDB and Cassandra store data that does not fit neat tables.

In-memory databases such as Redis and SAP HANA keep data in RAM for very fast answers. Distributed databases spread data over many servers so that one failure does not stop the service.

Features of a DBMS. Data storage in tables; quick data retrieval with simple commands; data manipulation (add, change, delete); data integrity (rules such as "marks must be 0 to 100"); control of redundancy (each fact stored once); security (who may see or change what); and backup and recovery.

Advantages of a DBMS Disadvantages (challenges)
fast storage, searching and retrieval needs trained people to set up and manage
reduces repetition of data (redundancy) software, hardware and training cost money
keeps data consistent and accurate a badly managed system is a security risk
many users can work at the same time large systems need regular maintenance
security through passwords and permissions very large data can make it slow without tuning
backup and recovery after accidents a failure of the server stops every user

A spreadsheet such as Excel is fine for one person's small list, but it cannot stop two rows having the same roll number, does not link tables safely, slows down with hundreds of thousands of rows, and is awkward for many users at once. A DBMS does all of these.

Relational DBMS (RDBMS)

A Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) is a DBMS that stores data in tables (relations) of rows and columns and links the tables through common fields called keys. MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server are RDBMSs.

Eight advantages of a DBMS, explained

  1. Fast storage and retrieval. A query such as SELECT * FROM students WHERE roll = 5 finds one record among thousands in a fraction of a second. A paper register may take minutes. Indexes make the search quicker still.
  2. Less data redundancy. Each fact is stored once, so the address of a student is not repeated in the library, fee and exam files. This saves space and avoids mismatched copies.
  3. Data consistency and accuracy. When the address is changed in one place, every report shows the new one. Rules such as CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100) stop wrong values from being entered.
  4. Data security. Users get passwords and permissions, so a class teacher can read marks but only the examination head can change them. This protects private records such as the citizenship numbers kept by a bank.
  5. Multi-user access. Many people can use the same data at the same time, as thousands of voters check their names on the Election Commission website. The DBMS controls the changes so that they do not clash.
  6. Backup and recovery. The DBMS keeps copies and logs of the changes, so data can be restored after a power failure or a crash. A bank cannot lose a transaction.
  7. Data integrity through keys. A primary key prevents two students with the same roll number, and a foreign key prevents a mark from being saved for a student who does not exist.
  8. Easy reports and decision making. With GROUP BY and COUNT the school finds the number of students by district or the average mark of each subject. The principal gets the report in one command.

2.2 Data types in MySQL: numeric, string and date/time types

Data type

The data type of a column decides what kind of value it may hold (whole number, decimal, text, date), how much space each value takes, and which operations make sense on it.

Choosing the right type keeps wrong data out and saves space: a date column rejects "hello", and arithmetic works on numbers but not on names.

Numeric types

Type Holds Range or note
TINYINT very small whole numbers −128 to 127
SMALLINT small whole numbers −32,768 to 32,767
INT whole numbers −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647
BIGINT very large whole numbers about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸
DECIMAL(p, s) exact numbers with decimals p digits in total, s after the point; use for money and marks
FLOAT, DOUBLE approximate numbers with decimals very large or tiny values, small rounding errors

String (character) types

Type Holds Note
CHAR(n) fixed-length text, up to 255 characters always uses the space of n characters; good for codes such as gender 'M'/'F'
VARCHAR(n) variable-length text, up to n characters uses only as much space as the text; best for names and addresses
TEXT long text, up to 65,535 bytes paragraphs, comments, descriptions

Date and time types (written in quotes, in this exact order)

Type Format Example
DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD' '2010-03-12'
TIME 'hh:mm:ss' '14:30:00'
DATETIME 'YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss' '2025-07-17 10:15:00'
TIMESTAMP like DATETIME, stored in UTC; can fill itself in automatically used to record when a row was created or changed

BOOLEAN stores TRUE or FALSE. In MySQL it is really TINYINT(1): TRUE is stored as 1 and FALSE as 0.

Worked example 2.1 — watching data types at work

Problem. A table has phone_int INT, phone_txt VARCHAR(10), code_char CHAR(5), price_dec DECIMAL(8,2) and joined DATE. Predict, then check in MySQL, what happens to each value:(a) the mobile number 9800000001 in phone_int;(b) 1234.567 in price_dec;(c) 'ABCDEFG' in code_char;(d) '2007 ' in joined.

Solution. (a) The largest INT is 2,147,483,647, so a ten-digit Nepali mobile number does not fit:

ERROR 1264 (22003): Out of range value for column 'phone_int' at row 1

Phone numbers are labels, not quantities, so they belong in VARCHAR(10) (or CHAR(10)), which also keeps a leading zero such as 01-5550000.

(b) DECIMAL(8,2) keeps two decimal places, so MySQL stores 1234.57 and gives a warning ("Data truncated").

(c) Seven characters do not fit in five:

ERROR 1406 (22001): Data too long for column 'code_char' at row 1

(d) A DATE must be a full 'YYYY-MM-DD':

ERROR 1292 (22007): Incorrect date value: '2007  ' for column 'joined' at row 1
DATE means an AD date

MySQL's DATE follows the Gregorian (AD) calendar.

A Bikram Sambat date such as '2081-03-32' (Asar 32) is rejected because no AD month has 32 days, and worse, '2082-04-15' is accepted — as 15 April 2082 AD, which makes every age or day-of-week calculation wrong.

Store AD dates in DATE columns; if you must keep the BS date, store it in a separate CHAR(10) column. (An example like 2047-07-06 is a BS date formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.)

2.3 Table: field, record and table design

Table, field and record

A table is the basic structure of a relational database: data about one kind of thing (students, books, products) arranged in rows and columns.

A field (column) holds one kind of fact for every row, such as Name or Date of Birth, and has a fixed data type. A record (row) holds all the facts about one item — one student, one book — so a record is one complete entry.

Key points about tables, fields and records:

  • A table holds one kind of entity; its columns are fields and its rows are records. The table is the primary building block of a database.
  • Every field has a name (such as dob) and a data type (such as DATE); every value in that field must fit the type.
  • Each record describes one entity completely and is usually identified by a unique ID, the primary key.
  • Tables can be linked to other tables through keys (section 2.4).

Designing a table

A well-designed table answers questions correctly for years. Follow these steps:

  1. Decide the entity the table is about (students, books, sales).
  2. List the fields, one fact per field: separate name, class and district rather than one long "details" field.
  3. Choose a data type and size for each field.
  4. Choose the primary key, a field whose value is different for every record (roll number, book number).
  5. Add constraints such as NOT NULL for fields that must always be filled.
  6. Do not store what can be calculated. Store the date of birth, not the age (the age changes every year); store marks, not the total.
Worked example 2.2 — designing a library table

Problem. Design a table books for the school library to store the book number, title, author, price, number of copies and the date each book was bought. Give each field a suitable data type and choose the primary key.

Solution.

Field Data type Reason
book_no INT (primary key) a unique number for every book
title VARCHAR(100), NOT NULL titles vary in length; every book has one
author VARCHAR(60) names vary in length
price DECIMAL(7,2) money needs exact decimals, e.g. 545.50
copies SMALLINT a small whole number
bought_on DATE an AD date such as '2025-04-20' 
CREATE TABLE books (
    book_no   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    title     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    author    VARCHAR(60),
    price     DECIMAL(7, 2),
    copies    SMALLINT,
    bought_on DATE
);

2.4 Keys and relationships

In a database, keys are fields (or groups of fields) that identify records uniquely and link tables together.

The keys you must know
  • A primary key is the field (or combination of fields) that uniquely identifies each record of a table. Its values must be unique and never NULL, and a table has only one primary key.
  • A candidate key is any field or set of fields that could serve as the primary key because it is unique and never empty. One candidate is chosen as the primary key; the others are called alternate keys.
  • A composite key is a key made of two or more fields together, used when no single field is unique on its own.
  • A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It creates the link between the tables and makes sure the link is valid (referential integrity); it is the "linking pin" between tables.

In a students table, roll and a unique symbol_no (SEE symbol number) are both candidate keys. If roll is chosen as the primary key, symbol_no becomes an alternate key. name is not a candidate key, because two students can share a name.

A super key is any set of fields that is unique, even if it contains extra fields (such as roll + name); every candidate key is a minimal super key.

Primary key Foreign key
identifies each record of its own table refers to the primary key of another table
must be unique may repeat (one student has many marks)
can never be NULL may be NULL unless forbidden
only one per table a table may have several
example: roll in students example: roll in marks
Primary key uniqueness in a Library table

Two different books in a Library table can never share the same BookID B_01. If BookID is the primary key of the Library table, the DBMS will — the DBMS would reject the second row.

Each book needs its own BookID (B_01, B_02, …); it is the StudentID (the foreign key) that may repeat, because one student can borrow many books.

Worked example 2.3 — finding the keys

Problem. A table results has the fields symbol_no (unique for every student), roll, class, name and gpa, where a roll number is unique only within one class.(a) List the candidate keys.(b) Choose a primary key and name the alternate key.(c) Which key is composite?

Solution.(a) symbol_no on its own is unique; roll alone is not (Class 9 and Class 10 both have roll 1), but the pair (class, roll) is. So the candidate keys are symbol_no and (class, roll).(b) A single short field is simpler: choose symbol_no as the primary key; then (class, roll) is the alternate key.(c) (class, roll) is composite, because it is made of two fields.

Types of relationship

A relationship is a logical link between two tables through a common field (a key). It lets data stored in separate tables be used together without repeating it.

Relationship Meaning Example How it is stored
One-to-one (1 : 1) one record on each side links to exactly one on the other a person and a passport; a student and a library card the primary key of one table is a unique foreign key in the other
One-to-many (1 : M) one record links to many, but each of those links back to only one a teacher and the classes taught; a customer and orders; a student and marks the foreign key goes in the "many" table
Many-to-many (M : N) many on each side link to many on the other students and courses; books and authors a third junction table holds the pairs of keys

One-to-many is by far the most common relationship. A one-to-one link is used to split rarely-used or private details (medical records) into a separate table.

2.5 Introduction to MySQL

MySQL is a free, open-source relational DBMS that uses SQL (Structured Query Language) to define, store and query data.

It was first released in 1995 by the Swedish company MySQL AB, which was bought by Sun Microsystems in 2008; Oracle Corporation took it over with Sun in 2010 and maintains it today.

Most websites, school and office systems and many mobile apps keep their data in MySQL because it is fast, reliable and free.

Features of MySQL

  • Open source and free (Community Edition), and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.
  • Simple language: SQL commands read almost like English.
  • Data definition, retrieval and manipulation: create tables, query them and change their data.
  • Multi-user: many users and programs can work at the same time.
  • Security: user accounts, passwords and permissions.
  • Fast and scalable: from a school lab to websites with millions of users.
  • Works with modern applications: PHP, Python, Java and web frameworks.

Installing MySQL 8 on Windows

MySQL Installer on Windows was shipped for MySQL 8.0, whereas the current long-term support release is the series to install now is MySQL 8.4 LTS (long-term support, maintained until 2032), which installs from an ordinary MSI file and is set up with MySQL Configurator. Workbench is downloaded separately.

  1. Open dev.mysql.com/downloads/mysql, choose version 8.4 LTS and operating system Microsoft Windows, and download the Windows (x86, 64-bit), MSI Installer. Click "No thanks, just start my download".
  2. Run the downloaded .msi file and choose the Typical setup. At the end keep Run MySQL Configurator ticked and click Finish.
  3. In MySQL Configurator, keep the data folder, then on Type and Networking choose Development Computer and leave the port as 3306.
  4. On Accounts and Roles type a strong root password twice and remember it: you will need it every time you log in as root.
  5. On Windows Service keep "Configure MySQL Server as a Windows Service" (service name MySQL84) and "Start the MySQL Server at System Startup".
  6. Accept the defaults for file permissions and sample databases, then on Apply Configuration click Execute. When every step shows a green tick, click Finish.
  7. Download MySQL Workbench from dev.mysql.com/downloads/workbench, install it, and open it.
Check the installation

Open MySQL 8.4 Command Line Client from the Start menu (or a Command Prompt in C:\Program Files\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.4\bin) and type mysql --version — two hyphens and no spaces (no space between the two hyphens).

Then log in with mysql -u root -p, type your password, and you should see the mysql> prompt. Leave with exit;, quit; or Ctrl + D.

Working in MySQL Workbench

MySQL Workbench is the graphical tool for writing SQL and seeing the results. On its home screen, double-click the tile Local instance MySQL84, type the root password, and the SQL editor opens.

Error 1175: Workbench's safe-update mode

Workbench starts in safe-update mode, which refuses an UPDATE or DELETE whose WHERE clause does not use a key column. For example UPDATE students SET class = 10; stops with

ERROR 1175 (HY000): You are using safe update mode and you tried to update a table without a WHERE that uses a KEY column.

This protects you from changing every row by accident. Add a WHERE that uses the primary key (WHERE roll = 5), or, when you really mean every row, untick Edit → Preferences → SQL Editor → Safe Updates and reconnect.

SQL and queries

SQL and query

SQL (Structured Query Language), pronounced "S-Q-L" or "sequel", is the standard language for working with relational databases. It was developed at IBM in the 1970s. A query is one request written in SQL — to create a table, retrieve, insert, update or delete data.

Sub-language Purpose Commands
DDL — Data Definition Language define and change the structure CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME
DML — Data Manipulation Language work with the data inside tables INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE
DCL — Data Control Language control permissions GRANT, REVOKE
TCL — Transaction Control Language make a group of changes permanent or undo them COMMIT, ROLLBACK, START TRANSACTION

SQL keywords are not case-sensitive (select works like SELECT), but writing keywords in capitals makes queries easier to read. Every statement ends with a semicolon, and text and date values go in single quotes.

Constraints

Constraint

A constraint is a rule attached to a column or table that the DBMS enforces on every INSERT and UPDATE, so that only valid, consistent data enters the table.

Constraint Rule it enforces Example
PRIMARY KEY values unique and never NULL roll INT PRIMARY KEY
FOREIGN KEY value must exist in the referenced table FOREIGN KEY (roll) REFERENCES students(roll)
NOT NULL the column must always have a value name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
UNIQUE no two rows may have the same value (NULL allowed) phone VARCHAR(10) UNIQUE
CHECK the value must satisfy a condition (enforced from MySQL 8.0.16) CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
DEFAULT value used when none is given district VARCHAR(30) DEFAULT 'Kathmandu'

Constraints keep data accurate, stop duplicate or impossible entries, enforce the links between tables and record the organisation's rules inside the database itself.

2.6 Data Definition Language (DDL): CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE

DDL statements build and change the structure of the database: databases, tables, columns and constraints. They do not work on individual rows.

In MySQL every DDL statement is committed at once — it cannot be undone with ROLLBACK — so think before you run DROP or TRUNCATE.

CREATE

CREATE DATABASE school;
USE school;
CREATE TABLE students (
    roll     INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    gender   CHAR(1),
    class    INT NOT NULL,
    district VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Kathmandu',
    dob      DATE,
    CONSTRAINT chk_gender CHECK (gender IN ('M', 'F'))
);
DESCRIBE students;

USE selects the database that the following statements work on, and DESCRIBE (or DESC) shows the structure MySQL actually created:

Field Type Null Key Default Extra
roll int NO PRI NULL
name varchar(40) NO NULL
gender char(1) YES NULL
class int NO NULL
district varchar(20) YES Kathmandu
dob date YES NULL

SHOW DATABASES; lists the databases and SHOW TABLES; lists the tables of the current database.

ALTER

ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table. All of these were run, in this order, on the table above:

Task Statement
add a column ALTER TABLE students ADD email VARCHAR(50);
change a column's type or size ALTER TABLE students MODIFY COLUMN district VARCHAR(30);
rename a column and give its type ALTER TABLE students CHANGE dob date_of_birth DATE;
rename a column only (MySQL 8) ALTER TABLE students RENAME COLUMN date_of_birth TO dob;
delete a column ALTER TABLE students DROP COLUMN email;
set a default value ALTER TABLE students ALTER district SET DEFAULT 'Kathmandu';
remove a named constraint ALTER TABLE students DROP CONSTRAINT chk_gender;
add a constraint ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT chk_gender CHECK (gender IN ('M', 'F'));
rename the table ALTER TABLE students RENAME TO pupils; or RENAME TABLE students TO pupils;
MODIFY replaces the whole column definition

After ALTER TABLE students MODIFY COLUMN district VARCHAR(30); MySQL's DESCRIBE showed the default of district had changed from 'Kathmandu' to NULL: MODIFY rebuilds the column from exactly what you write, so anything you leave out (NOT NULL, DEFAULT) is lost.

Repeat it: MODIFY COLUMN district VARCHAR(30) DEFAULT 'Kathmandu'; — or put it back with ALTER … SET DEFAULT as in the table above.

DROP and TRUNCATE

CREATE TABLE notice (id INT, title VARCHAR(30));
INSERT INTO notice VALUES (1, 'Holiday'), (2, 'Exam routine');
TRUNCATE TABLE notice;
SELECT * FROM notice;

The SELECT now returns Empty set, but DESCRIBE notice; still shows both columns: TRUNCATE removed all the rows and kept the structure.

DROP TABLE notice;

Now SHOW TABLES; no longer lists notice: DROP removed the table and its data for ever. DROP DATABASE school; would remove the whole database.

DELETE TRUNCATE DROP
Type DML DDL DDL
Removes chosen rows (with WHERE) or all rows all rows the whole table: rows and structure
Structure kept? yes yes no
WHERE allowed? yes no no
Can be rolled back? yes, inside a transaction no no
Speed on big tables slower (row by row) very fast very fast

2.7 Data Manipulation Language (DML): INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE

DML statements work on the data inside tables without changing their structure.

All the examples below use the students table built in §2.6 (with district widened to VARCHAR(30)) and follow one another in order, so each result is exactly what MySQL returned at that point.

INSERT — adding records

INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, ...) VALUES (value1, value2, ...);
INSERT INTO table_name VALUES (value1, value2, ...);   -- a value for every column, in order

INSERT INTO students (roll, name, gender, class, district, dob)
VALUES (1, 'Aarosh Pokharel', 'M', 10, 'Kathmandu', '2010-03-12');

INSERT INTO students (roll, name, gender, class, district, dob) VALUES
(2, 'Subigya Nepal', 'F', 10, 'Lalitpur', '2010-07-25'),
(3, 'Binay Adhikari', 'M', 10, 'Kaski', '2009-11-02'),
(4, 'Nidhi Sharma', 'F', 9, 'Chitwan', '2011-01-19'),
(5, 'Sampada Bhattarai', 'F', 10, 'Kathmandu', '2010-05-30'),
(6, 'Aman Yadav', 'M', 9, 'Dhanusha', '2011-09-14'),
(7, 'Rajesh Tamang', 'M', 10, 'Makwanpur', NULL),
(8, 'Anjali Gurung', 'F', 9, 'Kaski', '2011-02-21'),
(9, 'Iman Shrestha', 'M', 9, 'Bhaktapur', '2011-08-03');

INSERT INTO students VALUES (10, 'Muna Rai', 'F', 10, 'Morang', '2010-04-27');
INSERT INTO students (roll, name, class) VALUES (11, 'Dikshya Pokhrel', 10);
SELECT * FROM students;
roll name gender class district dob

2 Subigya Nepal F 10 Lalitpur 2010-07-25

The second INSERT added eight rows in one statement. Dikshya's row shows the constraints at work: district received its DEFAULT 'Kathmandu', and the columns with no value and no default became NULL ("no value").

Worked example 2.4 — inserts the DBMS refuses

Problem. Predict the result of each statement on the table above.(a) INSERT INTO students (roll, name, class) VALUES (3, 'Kiran Thapa', 9);(b) INSERT INTO students (roll, name) VALUES (12, 'Kiran Thapa');(c) INSERT INTO students (roll, name, gender, class) VALUES (12, 'Kiran Thapa', 'X', 9);

Solution. Each one breaks a constraint, so MySQL rejects the whole row:

(a) ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '3' for key 'students.PRIMARY'
(b) ERROR 1364 (HY000): Field 'class' doesn't have a default value
(c) ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_gender' is violated.

(a) roll 3 already exists, and a primary key must be unique.(b) class is NOT NULL and has no default.(c) the CHECK allows only 'M' or 'F'.

SELECT — retrieving data

SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name
WHERE condition
ORDER BY column [ASC | DESC];

SELECT * returns every column; the answer comes back as a temporary table called the result set. Dikshya's practice row is removed first with DELETE FROM students WHERE roll = 11;, leaving ten students.

The WHERE clause keeps only the rows for which its condition is true. It can use the comparison operators =, <> (not equal), >, <, >=, <=, the logical operators AND, OR, NOT, and the special forms BETWEEN … AND …, IN (…) and IS NULL.

Worked example 2.5 — filtering rows with WHERE

Problem. Write queries to list(a) the name and date of birth of Class 10 students,(b) the roll and name of girls in Class 10,(c) students from Kaski or Chitwan,(d) students born in 2010,(e) students from the three districts of Kathmandu Valley,(f) students whose date of birth is missing.

Solution.

(a)

SELECT name, dob FROM students WHERE class = 10;
name dob
Aarosh Pokharel 2010-03-12
Subigya Nepal 2010-07-25
Binay Adhikari 2009-11-02
Sampada Bhattarai 2010-05-30
Rajesh Tamang NULL
Muna Rai 2010-04-27

(b)

SELECT roll, name FROM students WHERE gender = 'F' AND class = 10;
roll name
2 Subigya Nepal
5 Sampada Bhattarai
10 Muna Rai

(c)

SELECT name, district FROM students WHERE district = 'Kaski' OR district = 'Chitwan';
name district
Binay Adhikari Kaski
Nidhi Sharma Chitwan
Anjali Gurung Kaski

(d)

SELECT name, dob FROM students WHERE dob BETWEEN '2010-01-01' AND '2010-12-31';
name dob
Aarosh Pokharel 2010-03-12
Subigya Nepal 2010-07-25
Sampada Bhattarai 2010-05-30

(e)

SELECT name, district FROM students WHERE district IN ('Kathmandu', 'Lalitpur', 'Bhaktapur');

Aarosh Pokharel Kathmandu
Subigya Nepal Lalitpur
Sampada Bhattarai Kathmandu
Iman Shrestha Bhaktapur

(f)

LIKE — searching for patterns

LIKE compares text with a pattern that contains wildcard characters: % stands for any number of characters (including none) and _ (underscore) stands for exactly one character. The pattern must match the whole value.

With MySQL's default settings LIKE ignores the difference between capital and small letters.

Pattern Matches Example values
'A%' starts with A Aarosh, Aman, Anil
'%rai' ends with rai Muna Rai, Sampada Bhattarai
'%sh%' contains sh anywhere Aarosh, Rajesh, Shrestha
'_a%' second letter is a Sampada, Rajesh
'_man' exactly four letters ending in man Aman, Iman

UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes every row

UPDATE students SET class = 10; puts every student in Class 10, and DELETE FROM students; empties the table. Write the WHERE clause first, and test it with a SELECT that uses the same condition before you run the UPDATE or DELETE.

DELETE — removing records

DELETE FROM table_name WHERE condition;

DELETE FROM students WHERE roll = 11; removed Dikshya's row (1 row affected), DELETE FROM students WHERE name LIKE '%esh'; would remove every student whose name ends in "esh", and DELETE FROM students; would remove all rows while keeping the table's structure.

MySQL normally runs with autocommit switched on (SELECT @@autocommit; returns 1): each INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE is saved permanently the moment it runs. To be able to undo, start a transaction first:

START TRANSACTION;
DELETE FROM students WHERE class = 9;      -- Query OK, 4 rows affected
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students;             -- 6
ROLLBACK;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students;             -- 10 again

ROLLBACK undid the delete; COMMIT would have made it permanent.

Common SQL syntax pitfalls to avoid
  1. Activity 5(a) inserts the date '2007 '; MySQL rejects it with error 1292 because a DATE must be 'YYYY-MM-DD', and the explanation then calls it 1990.
  2. Activity 5(b) says column names are "not specified", but (ID, Name) is a column list; and because Activity 3 made Class NOT NULL, this insert actually fails with error 1364.
  3. Activity 4(c) selects FROM record; the table is students.
  4. Activity 6(c) uses a column called rank. RANK is a reserved word in MySQL 8, so UPDATE record SET rank = rank + 1 … stops with a syntax error (1064). Rename the column, or write it in backquotes: `rank`.
  5. Activity 7(b) DELETE FROM students WHERE ID > 5; deletes rows whose ID is greater than 5, not "rank".
  6. In standard SQL transactions, DML changes require COMMIT to be saved permanently; in MySQL autocommit is on by default, so they are saved at once; only inside START TRANSACTION do you need COMMIT.

Reports

A report in MySQL is the organised presentation of data drawn from one or more tables by a query: a class list, a result summary, a sales total.

MySQL itself prints reports as plain result tables; for designed, printable or graphical reports the data is passed to tools such as Power BI, Tableau or Looker Studio. Reports help people understand data, plan and decide.

Type of report What it shows SQL used
Detail report the individual records SELECT … ORDER BY
Filtered report only records meeting a condition WHERE
Summary (aggregate) report totals, averages, counts COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN
Grouped report one summary line per group (class, district, subject) GROUP BY

The aggregate functions turn many rows into one value: COUNT(*) counts rows, SUM() adds, AVG() averages, MAX() and MIN() find the largest and smallest. GROUP BY makes one line per group, and HAVING filters groups.

To report marks, a second table holds each student's marks, with a composite primary key and a foreign key to students:

CREATE TABLE marks (
    roll    INT,
    subject VARCHAR(20),
    marks   INT CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
    PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject),
    FOREIGN KEY (roll) REFERENCES students(roll)
);
INSERT INTO marks VALUES
(1, 'Computer', 88), (1, 'Maths', 76), (2, 'Computer', 92), (2, 'Maths', 81),
(3, 'Computer', 67), (3, 'Maths', 58), (5, 'Computer', 95), (5, 'Maths', 89),
(7, 'Computer', 54), (7, 'Maths', 47), (10, 'Computer', 79), (10, 'Maths', 85);

The keys now protect the data. INSERT INTO marks VALUES (15, 'Computer', 70); fails with error 1452 ("a foreign key constraint fails") because there is no student 15; DELETE FROM students WHERE roll = 1; fails with error 1451 because marks still refer to roll 1; and INSERT INTO marks VALUES (4, 'Computer', 105); fails the CHECK (error 3819).

Project — database for the "KrishiKranti" farming app

In this case study, we design the database of a farming app ("KrishiKranti") that helps Nepali farmers manage crops, tools, sales and farm activities (the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development's site, doanepal.gov.np, has real crop data).

Write the report under the headings Introduction, Problem statement, Objective, SQL integration, Expected outcomes and Conclusion. A starting design with five entities, tested on MySQL 8.4:

CREATE DATABASE krishikranti;
USE krishikranti;
CREATE TABLE farmers (
    farmer_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name        VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    phone       VARCHAR(10) UNIQUE,
    district    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    land_ropani DECIMAL(6, 2) CHECK (land_ropani > 0)
);
CREATE TABLE crops (
    crop_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    crop_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    season    VARCHAR(10) CHECK (season IN ('Summer', 'Winter', 'Spring'))
);
CREATE TABLE tools (
    tool_id        INT PRIMARY KEY,
    farmer_id      INT NOT NULL,
    tool_name      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    tool_condition VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'Good',
    FOREIGN KEY (farmer_id) REFERENCES farmers(farmer_id)
);
CREATE TABLE sales (
    sale_id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
    farmer_id   INT NOT NULL,
    crop_id     INT NOT NULL,
    sale_date   DATE NOT NULL,
    quantity_kg DECIMAL(8, 2) CHECK (quantity_kg > 0),
    rate_per_kg DECIMAL(8, 2) CHECK (rate_per_kg > 0),
    FOREIGN KEY (farmer_id) REFERENCES farmers(farmer_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (crop_id) REFERENCES crops(crop_id)
);
CREATE TABLE farm_activities (
    activity_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    farmer_id     INT NOT NULL,
    crop_id       INT NOT NULL,
    activity      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    activity_date DATE NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (farmer_id) REFERENCES farmers(farmer_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (crop_id) REFERENCES crops(crop_id)
);

Every table uses the constraints the project asks for (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK) and foreign keys link sales, tools and activities to farmers and crops (one farmer — many sales).

With two sample farmers, the query SELECT sale_id, quantity_kg * rate_per_kg AS amount_rs FROM sales; returned 57750.0000 for 1,500 kg of paddy at Rs 38.50 per kg.

Now insert at least 25 records in each table, as the project requires, and write five report queries of your own.

2. Short questions — model answers

a. Data are raw, unprocessed facts and figures with no clear meaning on their own, e.g. 45, 67, 89. Information is data processed into a meaningful form, e.g. "the class average is 67".

b. A primary key is the field (or fields) whose value uniquely identifies each record of a table. It must be unique and cannot be NULL, and a table has only one, e.g. roll in a students table.

c. A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, linking the two and allowing only values that exist there, e.g. roll in the marks table refers to roll in students.

d. A field (column) holds one kind of fact for every record, e.g. Name. A row (record) holds all the facts about one entity, e.g. one student's roll, name, class and date of birth.

e. A database is an organised collection of related data, e.g. a school's tables of students and marks. A DBMS is the software that creates and manages that database, e.g. MySQL. The database is the data; the DBMS is the program that stores, retrieves and protects it.

f. An RDBMS is a DBMS that stores data in tables of rows and columns and links tables through keys (primary and foreign keys). Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server.

g. A DBMS stops duplicate and invalid data with keys and constraints, links related tables, handles very large amounts of data quickly, lets many users work at the same time, controls who can see or change data, and provides backup and recovery — none of which a simple spreadsheet does well.

h. The primary key gives every record a unique identity so that it can be found, updated or deleted without confusion. The foreign key links a record to a record in another table and makes sure the link points to a record that exists (referential integrity).

i. In a one-to-many relationship one record in the first table is linked to many records in the second, but each of those is linked to only one record in the first.

Example one customer places many orders on Daraz, but each order belongs to one customer.

j. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE) defines and changes the structure of the database — tables, columns, constraints. DML (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE) works on the data stored inside the tables.

k. WHERE filters the rows of a SELECT: only rows that satisfy its condition appear in the result, e.g. SELECT name FROM students WHERE class = 10; lists only Class 10 students.

l. SQL constraints are rules on columns — PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT — that the DBMS checks on every insert and update.

They keep data integrity by refusing duplicates, missing values, impossible values and links to records that do not exist.

m. A composite key is a key made of two or more fields that together identify a record uniquely. It is needed when no single field is unique, e.g. in a marks table neither roll nor subject is unique, but (roll, subject) is.

3. Long questions — model answers

a. DBMS and its advantages. A DBMS is software that creates, stores, retrieves, updates and deletes data in a database while keeping it consistent, secure and available to many users, e.g. MySQL or Oracle.

Advantages: (1) fast storage, searching and retrieval; (2) reduced redundancy — each fact stored once; (3) consistency and integrity through keys and constraints; (4) security through accounts and permissions; (5) many users at the same time; (6) backup and recovery after mistakes or failures.

b. Importance and features of the primary key. Without a primary key two records could look identical, and a DBMS could not tell which one to update, delete or link to; the primary key gives each record a unique identity and is the field that foreign keys refer to. Features: it uniquely identifies each record; it cannot contain duplicate values; it cannot be NULL; a table has only one primary key; it may be a single field or a composite of several fields.

c. DDL and DML.

DDL DML
Data Definition Language Data Manipulation Language
defines and changes the structure works on the data inside tables
CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE
affects whole tables and columns affects rows (records)
committed at once; cannot be rolled back can be rolled back inside a transaction
e.g. CREATE TABLE students (...) e.g. INSERT INTO students VALUES (...)

d. Table and query.

Table Query
a stored structure of rows and columns that holds the data a request written in SQL to work with that data
permanent; stays in the database runs when executed; its result set is temporary
created with CREATE TABLE written with SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
holds all the records of one entity can pick, filter, sort, combine and summarise records from many tables
e.g. students e.g. SELECT name FROM students WHERE class = 10;

e. Relationships. A relationship is a logical link between two tables based on a common field (a key), so that related data stored separately can be used together without repetition.

(1) One-to-one: one record on each side, e.g. a person and a passport. (2) One-to-many: one record linked to many, each of which links back to only one, e.g. a teacher and the classes taught.

(3) Many-to-many: many records on each side, e.g. students and courses; it is stored through a junction table such as enrolment(roll, course_code).

f. Query and its importance. A query is a request to the database, written in SQL, to retrieve, insert, update or delete data.

Importance: it retrieves exactly the data needed from large tables; filters rows with conditions; sorts and summarises data for reports; adds, changes and removes records without searching by hand; and combines data from several tables.

g. Report in MySQL and its purpose. A report is the organised presentation of data retrieved from one or more tables by SQL queries, e.g. a class list or a result summary.

MySQL produces it as a result table; tools such as Power BI or Tableau turn it into a printed or graphical report.

Its purpose is to help people understand and analyse data and make plans and decisions — summary, detail, grouped, filtered and aggregate reports serve different needs.

h. Report and its features. A report presents selected, organised data from a database in readable form.

Features: organised presentation; filtering of only the rows needed; summarisation with SUM, AVG, COUNT, MAX and MIN; grouping by class, district or subject; combination of data from several tables; timely access to current data; easy export to spreadsheets and reporting tools.

Chapter summary

  • Data are raw facts; information is processed, meaningful data. A database is an organised collection of related data; a DBMS (MySQL, Oracle) is the software that manages it; an RDBMS keeps data in linked tables.
  • DBMS advantages: fast retrieval, less redundancy, consistency, security, multi-user access, backup. Disadvantages: cost, expertise, maintenance.
  • Data types: INT, SMALLINT, BIGINT, DECIMAL(p,s) (exact), FLOAT (approximate); CHAR(n) (fixed), VARCHAR(n) (variable), TEXT; DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD', TIME, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP; BOOLEAN = TINYINT(1).
  • A table has fields (columns) and records (rows). Keys: primary (unique, not NULL, one per table), candidate, alternate, composite (two or more fields), foreign (refers to another table's primary key).
  • Relationships: 1 : 1, 1 : M (most common), M : N (via a junction table).
  • Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT.
  • DDL: CREATE, ALTER (ADD, MODIFY, CHANGE, RENAME COLUMN, DROP COLUMN), DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME — committed at once.
  • DML: INSERT, SELECT (WHERE, ORDER BY ASC/DESC, LIKE with % and _), UPDATE … SET … WHERE, DELETE … WHERE. Never forget WHERE.
  • Reports use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN with GROUP BY. Install MySQL 8.4 LTS with MySQL Configurator; write SQL in Workbench.

Answers to Group C

1. A database is an organised collection of related data; a DBMS is the software that creates and manages it (1).

Any three features (1 each): data stored in tables of rows and columns; quick retrieval with queries; data manipulation (insert, update, delete); integrity rules such as constraints; control of redundancy; security through accounts and permissions; backup and recovery.

2.

CREATE TABLE products (
    pid      INT PRIMARY KEY,
    pname    VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    category VARCHAR(20),
    price    DECIMAL(8, 2) CHECK (price > 0),
    qty      INT DEFAULT 0
);
INSERT INTO products (pid, pname, category, price, qty)
VALUES (6, 'Speaker', 'Audio', 1500.00, 10);
SELECT pname, price FROM products WHERE price > 500 ORDER BY price DESC;
DELETE FROM products WHERE qty = 0;

Tested with five more products (a mouse at Rs 450 and a headphone at Rs 1,850 were out of stock), the SELECT listed Webcam 2500.00, Headphone 1850.00, Speaker 1500.00, Keyboard 1200.00, Pen drive 32 GB 650.00 — the Rs 450 mouse is left out — and the DELETE reported 2 rows affected.

3. A key is a field or set of fields used to identify records uniquely and to link tables (1).

Primary key uniquely identifies each record, unique and not NULL, one per table — roll in students.

Foreign key a field that refers to the primary key of another table — roll in marks refers to students(roll).

Composite key two or more fields that together identify a record — (roll, subject) in marks.

4.

One-to-one each record on one side matches exactly one on the other, e.g. Person — Passport (draw two boxes joined by a line marked 1 and 1).

One-to-many one record matches many, each of which matches only one, e.g. Teacher — Class (marked 1 and M); the foreign key goes in the Class table.

Many-to-many many on each side, e.g. Student — Course; it is drawn and stored as Student 1 — M Enrolment M — 1 Course, with the junction table Enrolment holding (roll, course_code). (See the figure in §2.4.)

Model answer D1: database, DBMS and its advantages (10 marks)

Introduction. Data are raw facts, information is processed data that has meaning, and a database is an organised collection of related data stored so that it can be retrieved easily.

A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that creates the database, stores data in it, and lets users search, change and protect it. MySQL, Oracle, MS Access and PostgreSQL are examples.

Advantages.

  1. Fast storage and retrieval of data.
  2. Less data redundancy (repetition).
  3. Consistency and accuracy of data.
  4. Security through passwords and permissions.
  5. Many users can share the data at the same time.
  6. Backup and recovery after a failure.
  7. Integrity through primary and foreign keys.
  8. Quick reports for decisions.

Disadvantages. A DBMS needs trained staff; the software, hardware and training cost money; a badly managed system is a security risk; it needs regular maintenance; and a failure of the server stops every user.

Point File system DBMS
Storage Separate files for each program One shared database
Redundancy High Low
Consistency Poor, copies differ Good
Security Weak Strong, with permissions
Searching Slow, manual Fast, by SQL
Example Card catalogue, paper register MySQL

Conclusion. A DBMS replaces scattered registers with one organised, safe and shared store of data, which is why schools, banks and government offices depend on one.

Model answer D2: DDL and DML commands (10 marks)

Introduction. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to talk to a relational database. Its commands are grouped by purpose; the two primary groups studied here are DDL, which defines the structure, and DML, which handles the data.

DDL (Data Definition Language).

Command Purpose Example
CREATE Makes a table CREATE TABLE students (roll INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, gender CHAR(1), class INT NOT NULL, district VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Kathmandu');
ALTER Changes the structure ALTER TABLE students ADD phone VARCHAR(10);
DROP Deletes the table and its data DROP TABLE notice;
TRUNCATE Deletes all rows, keeps the structure TRUNCATE TABLE notice;

DML (Data Manipulation Language).

  1. INSERT adds rows: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1, 'Sushmita', 'F', 10, 'Kathmandu');
  2. SELECT reads rows: SELECT name, district FROM students WHERE class = 10 ORDER BY name; gives Bibek (Lalitpur), Rohan (Kathmandu) and Sushmita (Kathmandu).
  3. UPDATE changes values: UPDATE marks SET marks = 60 WHERE roll = 4 AND subject = 'Computer'; changes Rohan's 54 to 60.
  4. DELETE removes rows: DELETE FROM marks WHERE roll = 3; leaves five rows in the marks table.

Aggregate and group queries. SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(marks), MAX(marks), MIN(marks) FROM marks WHERE subject = 'Computer'; returns 4, 75.25, 92 and 54. SELECT district, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY district; gives Bhaktapur 1, Kathmandu 2 and Lalitpur 1.

Point DDL DML
Works on Structure of tables Data inside tables
Commands CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE
Example CREATE TABLE INSERT INTO

Conclusion. DDL builds the empty container and DML fills it and asks questions of it; together they cover everything a school database needs.

Model answer D3: keys, relationships and joining tables (10 marks)

Introduction. A key is a field, or a set of fields, that identifies records or links tables. Keys make a relational database accurate and connected.

  1. Primary key: a field whose value is unique and never empty, so it identifies one record. roll in students is the primary key.
  2. Candidate key: any field that could serve as the primary key, such as a citizenship number.
  3. Composite key: a primary key of two or more fields. In marks the pair (roll, subject) is the key, because one student has one mark in each subject.
  4. Foreign key: a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. marks.roll refers to students.roll, so a mark cannot be saved for a student that does not exist.
  5. Unique key: allows no repeated values, such as a phone number.

Relationships. A one-to-one relationship joins one record to one record (a student and a library card). A one-to-many relationship joins one record to many (one student has many marks; this is the commonest).

A many-to-many relationship joins many to many (students and clubs) and is made with a third linking table.

Join query. To show the name with each mark of 80 or more:

SELECT students.name, marks.subject, marks.marks
FROM students JOIN marks ON students.roll = marks.roll
WHERE marks.marks >= 80
ORDER BY marks.marks DESC;
name subject marks
Bibek Computer 92
Sushmita Computer 88
Bibek Maths 81

The ON condition matches each foreign key with its primary key.

Point Primary key Foreign key
Purpose Identifies a record Links to another table
Duplicates Not allowed Allowed
Null Not allowed Allowed
Per table One Many

Conclusion. Primary keys identify, foreign keys connect, and a join uses them to bring the facts of several tables together.
